By "the last humans," do you mean that we'll change so much that we'll become a different species? Because "species" has a biological definition. By "we" do you mean a certain generation? The people of a certain nation? In both cases, I would probably say that "we" won't be the last generation because people will continue to reproduce (very wealthy nations, for instance, still produce children, just not as readily as poor nations), even as they get access to better and better medicine (that will potentially extend their lives indefinitely, even turning back the clock on aging) and better and better technology, that will, conceivably, remove all human drudgery. Our species will not change, at least not for a very, very long time. We will remain homo sapiens. Our DNA has not significantly changed in about 150,000 years; there's no reason to assume it will do so during the current generation.

If you mean that we'll be unrecognizable socially compared to previous generations, I would say that has already happened several times. Our ancestors took shelter in caves, wore loincloths made from fur, and hunted herbivores with sharpened sticks on the African Savannah. Now we sit comfortably wearing machine-made garments, in air-conditioned and artificially-lit buildings, reading and tapping on handheld computers for pleasure before we go back to the computer screen in front of us to do our work. The only "hunting" the majority of us modern humans do is at the supermarket (though some of us still hunt for the thrill of it, or to keep our survival skills sharp).

In the sense that technological change is exponential, humans a few hundred years from now are likely to be virtually unrecognizable socially, but will still be almost exactly the same genetically. This is assuming, of course, that there doesn't become available some kind of vast life-altering technology, readily available to all, which allows one to alter one's genotype and phenotype radically on the fly, allowing one to augment one's body in ways that would be unthinkable now (such as growing crocodile skin or giant bird wings, for example). This isn't completely out of the question, given the advancements in gene therapy even over the last 15 years.

My guess is that before humans are able to genetically alter themselves to the point that we become a new species, we will have created a superhuman A.I. with the ability to augment its own general intelligence indefinitely. Once that happens, we will essentially have created a god on Earth, and our species' existence is likely to become extremely precarious. As Sam Harris argues, even if we created a completely benign self-augmenting A.I., once its goals even slightly differed from our own, we'd be in trouble. The "singularity" you're talking about? It's likely to take that form, and I am honestly not as optimistic about the coming A.I. overlords as others might be.
